title: Asymmetric KV Residency Model and Page Migration Sketch
body:
Purpose and context:

This note lays out a lightweight, implementation-forward sketch for an asymmetric residency model for the KV cache plus a page-migration and PCIe-aware throttling policy. The goal is to reduce end-to-end token latency variance and unit-cost by keeping the true hot working set on-attached device memory (GPU HBM), the warm working set resident in local host memory (NUMA-local DRAM), and cold entries either on remote host memory or persistent backing (NVMe). The design emphasizes: graceful degradation under PCIe bandwidth pressure, inexpensive telemetry, and compatibility with existing serving runtime kernel primitives (batching, KV cache lookups, and async I/O).

High-level idea:
- Classify entries into three residency tiers: HOT (GPU HBM), WARM (local host DRAM, same NUMA node as GPU), COLD (remote NUMA or disk).
- Maintain a single global scoring stream per model shard that feeds the migration machinery; scores are lightweight integers computed at request-time and updated asynchronously.
- Use PCIe and host memory bandwidth signals to gate migrations out of HOT or WARM when bus pressure is high (bandwidth-steering).
- Allow soft hysteresis windows to avoid oscillation (migrations must persist for a minimum dwell time unless forced eviction needed).

Residency scoring (sketch):
- Each KV key has three counters kept as 32-bit integers: recency_epoch, request_count, last_seq_seen.
- On lookup: increment request_count, set recency_epoch = current_epoch. current_epoch is a global monotonic tick updated every 50ms.
- Compute score S = request_count * alpha + max(0, (epoch_weight - (current_epoch - recency_epoch))) * beta - penalty, where penalty increases if page-ins for this key recently caused bus saturation.
- Tunable constants: alpha=1, beta=8, epoch_weight=4 (starting defaults). We experiment to find values.

Eviction/migration rules:
- Promotion HOT <- WARM: if S > PROMOTE_HOT && GPU_free_HBM > HOT_margin and PCIe_util < BUS_HIGH_WATER.
- Promotion WARM <- COLD: if S > PROMOTE_WARM && local_DRAM_free > WARM_margin.
- Demotion HOT -> WARM: when GPU_free_HBM < HOT_pressure_threshold OR (PCIe_util > BUS_CRITICAL and demotion_candidate_age > min_dwell_ms).
- Demotion WARM -> COLD: when host_DRAM_pressure_local > DRAM_CRITICAL or if entry score decays to below WARM_floor.

Default threshold suggestions (first-pass):
- BUS_HIGH_WATER: 70% measured PCIe H2D+D2H bandwidth utilization averaged over 200ms.
- BUS_CRITICAL: 92% sustained over 100ms.
- HOT_margin: reserve 5% HBM for emergent allocations (min_free_bytes = 0.05 * HBM_total).
- HOT_pressure_threshold: when free HBM < 8% or when swap-induced page faults per second > 200 for the device.
- DRAM_CRITICAL: local node DRAM usage > 88% for > 1s.
- min_dwell_ms: 250ms for HOT entries, 500ms for WARM entries (empirically reduce thrash).

PCIe-aware migration gating and bandwidth-steering:
- Runtime exposes two signals: instantaneous bandwidth (moving average 50ms) and a 1s window peak. These are inexpensive samplers from the device driver (or perf counters).
- If instantaneous bandwidth > BUS_HIGH_WATER: stall non-critical promotions and prioritize demotions of low-score HOT entries to reduce upcoming traffic.
- If bandwidth > BUS_CRITICAL: force immediate demotions of newest demotion candidates and escalate to local DRAM-only lookups (disable GPU page-ins for non-top-K requests).
- During heavy bus use the scheduler can convert a migration action into a deferred async fetch: respond to the next request with a staged fetch from local DRAM instead of GPU page-in. This keeps p99 latency bounded when PCIe is constrained.

Host paging implementation approaches (pros/cons):
1) Kernel-managed page migration using standard faults + madvise/migrate_pages: minimal kernel changes, but page-fault latency spikes and signal noise make SLO guarantees hard.
2) Userspace-managed pages via mmap + prefetch/io_uring: explicit async read-in of pages into a dedicated pinned pool in local NUMA DRAM. More control and predictable latency; requires a small glue layer in the runtime to manage pinned host slabs.
3) Hybrid: keep a small pinned host slab for serving; use madvise/MLOCK on that slab and prefetch into it using io_uring when promoting from COLD->WARM. Fall back to kernel faults for ad-hoc misses.

Recommendation: start with option (2) for experiment phase. Implement a lightweight host-slab allocator (per NUMA node) that the runtime owns; allocate slab pages with hugepages when available and register them to avoid CPU copying during async I/O. Use io_uring for low-latency async reads from backing store (NVMe) and madvise to advise kernel on lifespan.

NUMA and local affinity rules:
- Maintain per-GPU-affinity pools. For multi-GPU hosts use per-NUMA local DRAM to keep traffic on the same PCIe root complex. Avoid cross-NUMA promotions unless necessary.
- A simple placement rule: when promoting to WARM, allocate from the NUMA node local to the GPU's root complex; if free pool is empty, consider stealing from sibling nodes only if (PCIe_util < BUS_HIGH_WATER and remote_latency_penalty_estimate < steal_threshold).

Eviction policy: hybrid LFU-LRU with epoch decay:
- Use exponentially decayed request_count every decay_window (default 8s): request_count = floor(request_count * decay_factor) where decay_factor = 0.75.
- Maintain approximate LRU lists only at WARM and COLD tiers to make eviction O(1). HOT tier uses pinned slots ordered by last promotion time and score-based sampling for eviction candidates.

Telemetry and signals to collect:
- Per-second: PCIe bandwidth H2D and D2H, pcie-ops/sec, swap/page-in events (if kernel-based), host DRAM free per NUMA node, GPU HBM free.
- Per-request: key hit/miss, residency tier, migration action triggered, migration latency, and whether action was deferred due to bus pressure.
- Aggregate metrics for experiments: p50/p95/p99 latency for model token generation, tokens/sec, GPU_util, percentage of requests served entirely from HOT, and cost per million tokens (approx).

Microbench experiment plan (first round):
- Workloads: synthetic Zipfian key access (s=1.1), bursty session replay traces (from production sampling), and a mixed multi-tenant workload reproducing contention.
- Baselines: current naive paging + kernel faults; host-slab io_uring without bandwidth steering; host-slab + bandwidth-steering + asymmetric residency.
- Targets: reduce p99 latency tail by 20% compared to kernel faults baseline under 2x load, keep token cost within +/-10% of baseline in steady state, and reduce average PCIe bytes/token via more local hits.
- Success criteria: sustained p99 improvement on burst scenario; fewer PCIe page-ins during steady-state workloads.

Operational considerations and failure modes:
- Regression risk: scoring constants might over-promote large cold sets into WARM and cause host OOM. Mitigation: enforce hard caps per-tenant and global rate limit for promotions (token-bucket).
- Hot oscillation: use dwell times + decay factors; add promotion budget that refills slowly (e.g., 1 promotion per 5ms per shard).
- PCIe denial-of-service from multi-tenant noise: require per-tenant bandwidth budgets and enforce via scheduler at PCIe gateway (or by throttling migrations per tenant).
- Debugging: provide a "residency tracer" hook that can dump a shard's residency histogram and last-100 migration events. Persist tracer output to logs for postmortem.

Open questions / research items:
- Exact scoring weights: tune alpha/beta/epoch windows across models of different sequence lengths.
- How to integrate with existing kernel-level swap (host fallback) for air-gapped private deployments with stricter ops surface?
- Best heuristics to detect when a migration will be beneficial vs. simply stalling and serving from local DRAM (cost model needed).
- Can we use preemption hints from the GPU driver to schedule migrations during otherwise idle PCIe windows?

Next steps (concrete):
1) Implement a minimal host-slab manager and io_uring prefetch path in the runtime as an A/B feature behind a flag (2 engineer-weeks).
2) Add a simple score-based promoter/demoter with default thresholds and per-shard promotion budget (1 engineer-week).
3) Hook up PCIe bandwidth sampling (driver counters) and implement gating logic for promotions (1 engineer-week).
4) Run the microbench suite and collect telemetry; iterate thresholds and dwell times (2–3 weeks).
5) If promising, port the host-slab to use hugepages and add NUMA pinning (follow-up sprint).

Appendix: quick pseudocode for promotion decision (high level)

for each promotion_candidate in promotion_queue:
  if promotion_candidate.score < PROMOTE_HOT: continue
  if gpu_hbm_free < HOT_margin: continue
  if pcie_moving_avg > BUS_HIGH_WATER: defer(promotion_candidate)
  else perform_gpu_pagein_async(promotion_candidate)

Notes on implementation: page-in must be async and cancellable. Maintain a small in-flight limit per shard to avoid head-of-line blocking. When a page-in completes, bump the entry to HOT and mark dwell timer. If the page-in latency exceeds a threshold and downstream requests are waiting, satisfy them from WARM path (local DRAM) instead of waiting for GPU.

End.
